}{{{{\ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.06946pt}{-1.34427pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}}{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces
}{{{{\ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.06946pt}{-1.34427pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}}{}}}}^{(j)}(w)\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}H^{s_{3}}_{x}}

\displaystyle=\bigg\|\int_{0}^{t}\langle n\rangle^{s_{3}}\widehat{w}(n,t^{\prime})\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(j)}(t,t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}\bigg\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\ell^{2}_{n}}

\displaystyle\lesssim\|w\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{2}_{x}}\sup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\langle n\rangle^{s_{3}+2-\frac{1}{\theta}}

\displaystyle\lesssim\|w\|_{L^{1}_{T}L^{2}_{x}},

provided that
s_{3}\leq-2+\frac{1}{\theta}
.
By noting that
[\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\sim\langle n_{2}\rangle\gg\langle n\rangle

under
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}
,
we see that (
7.21
) is easily verified for
j=5
.

The sum for
\mathcal{A}^{(4)}_{n}(t,t^{\prime})
in (
7.7
)
is not absolutely convergent.
As in
[
48
]
,
we exploit the symmetry
n_{2}\leftrightarrow-n_{2}

and the oscillatory nature of the sine kernel.
Set

\displaystyle\Theta^{\pm}(n,n_{2}):=[\hskip-1.70717pt[n\pm n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]-[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\mp\frac{\langle n,n_{2}\rangle}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}.

(7.22)

Then,
noting that
[\hskip-1.70717pt[n\pm n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\sim[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\gg\langle n\rangle

under
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}
,
it follows from
(
2.7
) and the mean value theorem that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Theta^{\pm}(n,n_{2})&=\frac{|n|^{2}}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n\pm n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]+[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\pm\langle n,n_{2}\rangle\frac{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]-[\hskip-1.70717pt[n\pm n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}{([\hskip-1.70717pt[n\pm n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]+[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt])[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\\
&=O\bigg(\frac{\langle n\rangle^{2}}{\langle n_{2}\rangle}\bigg).\end{split}

(7.23)

Write

\sum_{n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\setminus\{0\}}F(n_{2})=\sum_{n_{2}\in\Lambda}\big(F(n_{2})+F(-n_{2})\big),

where the index
\Lambda
is as in (
1.22
).
Then,
from
(
7.7
), (
7.22
), the mean value theorem,
and (
7.23
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}&\mathcal{A}^{(4)}_{n}(t,t^{\prime})\\
&=e^{-(t-t^{\prime})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{\sin((t-t^{\prime})([\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]-[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]))+\sin((t-t^{\prime})([\hskip-1.70717pt[n-n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]-[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]))}{2[\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\\
&\hphantom{X}-e^{-(t-t^{\prime})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{\sin((t-t^{\prime})([\hskip-1.70717pt[n-n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]-[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]))}{2\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\bigg(\frac{1}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}-\frac{1}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n-n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\bigg)\\
&=e^{-(t-t^{\prime})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{2[\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\bigg\{\sin\bigg((t-t^{\prime})\Big(\frac{\langle n,n_{2}\rangle}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}+\Theta^{+}(n,n_{2})\Big)\bigg)\\
&\hphantom{XXXXX}-\sin\bigg((t-t^{\prime})\Big(\frac{\langle n,n_{2}\rangle}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}-\Theta^{-}(n,n_{2})\Big)\bigg)\bigg\}\\
&\hphantom{X}+O\bigg(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{\langle n\rangle}{\langle n_{2}\rangle^{4}}\bigg)\\
&\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n+n_{2}]\hskip-1.70717pt]\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\frac{\langle n\rangle^{2}}{\langle n_{2}\rangle}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{2}\in\Lambda\\
|n|\ll|n_{2}|^{\theta}\end{subarray}}\frac{\langle n\rangle}{\langle n_{2}\rangle^{4}}\\
&\lesssim\langle n\rangle^{2-\frac{1}{\theta}}\end{split}

(7.24)

for any
0\leq t^{\prime}\leq t\leq 1
and
0<\theta\leq 1
.
This proves (
7.21
) for
j=4
.

This completes the proof of Proposition
2.6
.
∎

We conclude this section by briefly discussing the regularity property
of the stochastic term
\mathbb{A}
defined in (
2.39
).
For this purpose, we first define its truncated version:

\displaystyle\mathbb{A}_{N}(x,t,t^{\prime})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}e_{n}(x)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=n_{1}+n_{2}\\
|n_{1}|\sim|n_{2}|\end{subarray}}e^{-\frac{t-t^{\prime}}{2}}\frac{\sin((t-t^{\prime})[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{1}]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{1}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\widehat{\Psi}_{N}(n_{1},t^{\prime})\widehat{\Psi}_{N}(n_{2},t).

(7.25)

Lemma 7.2
.

Let
\mathbb{A}_{N}(t,t^{\prime})
be as in (
7.25
).
Fix finite
q\geq 2
.
Then,
given any
T,\varepsilon>0
and finite
p\geq 1
,

\{\mathbb{A}_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
is a Cauchy sequence in
L^{p}(\Omega;L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})))
,
converging to some limit
\mathbb{A}

(
formally defined by (
2.39
)
)

in
L^{p}(\Omega;L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})))
,
where
\Delta_{2}(T)
is as in (
2.41
).
Moreover,
\mathbb{A}_{N}
converges almost surely to the same limit in
L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.
Furthermore,
we have
the following uniform tail estimate
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\mathbb{A}_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}_{x})}>\lambda\Big)\leq\begin{cases}C\exp\big(-c\frac{\lambda}{T^{\frac{1}{q}}}\big),&\text{when }0<T\leq 1,\\
CT\exp(-\lambda),&\text{when }T>1\end{cases}

(7.26)

for any
\lambda\gg 1
, and
N\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}
,
where
\mathbb{A}_{\infty}=\mathbb{A}
.

Proof.

As in the proof of Proposition
2.6
,
we only consider the case
0<T\leq 1
.
In the following, we simply study the regularity of
\mathbb{A}
, i.e. when
N=\infty
.
The claimed convergence and the tail estimate (
7.26
)
follow from a standard argument and the fact that
\mathbb{A}_{N}\in\mathcal{H}_{\leq 2}
,
N\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}
.
By comparing (
2.39
) with (
2.28
), we have

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbb{A}}(n,t,t^{\prime})=\mathcal{A}_{n,0}(t,t^{\prime})

for
(t,t^{\prime})\in\Delta_{2}(T)
.
Thus, from
(
7.6
)
and
(
7.7
), we can write

\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbb{A}}(n,t,t^{\prime})=\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(1)}(n,t,t^{\prime})+\mathbf{1}_{n=0}\cdot\Big(\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(3)}(0,t,t^{\prime})+\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(4)}(0,t,t^{\prime})+\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(5)}(0,t,t^{\prime})\Big),

where

\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(1)}(n,t,t^{\prime})=\mathcal{A}_{n,0}^{(1)}(t,t^{\prime})

and

\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(j)}(n,t,t^{\prime})=\mathcal{A}_{n}^{(j)}(t,t^{\prime})
,
j=3,4,5
.

From (
7.10
), we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(1)}(n,t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{q}_{t}([0,T])}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\langle n\rangle^{-3}T^{\frac{2}{q}}

for
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}
and
0\leq t^{\prime}\leq t\leq T
.
Note that, in (
2.39
),
t^{\prime}
appears
in
\sin((t-t^{\prime})[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{1}]\hskip-1.70717pt])

and
\Psi(n_{1},t^{\prime})
.
Then, proceeding as in the proof of Lemma 3.1 in
[
48
]
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(1)}(n,t,t^{\prime}_{1})-\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(1)}(n,t,t^{\prime}_{2})\|_{L^{q}_{t}([0,T])}^{2}\Big]\lesssim|t_{1}^{\prime}-t_{2}^{\prime}|^{\sigma_{0}}\langle n\rangle^{-3+\sigma_{0}}T^{\frac{2}{q}}

for some small
\sigma_{0}>0
.
Then, by
(a variant of) Lemma
3.7
, we
conclude that
\mathbb{A}^{(1)}\in L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})))

almost surely.
The exponential tail estimate (
7.26
) for

\mathbb{A}^{(1)}

follows from adapting the proof of Lemma
4.1
, using Lemma
3.8
.

It remains to estimate the deterministic terms

\mathbb{A}^{(j)}
,
j=3,4,5
, which appear only at the zeroth frequency.
Let
\phi
be a smooth bump function in Section
3

and set
\phi^{T}(t)=\phi(T^{-1}t)
.
Then, from (
7.16
), (
7.18
), (
7.19
),
Hausdorff-Young’s inequality,
and Young’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(3)}(0,t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T))}

\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{K}_{0}\|_{L^{q}_{T}}\leq\|\widehat{\phi^{T}\mathcal{K}_{0}}\|_{L^{q^{\prime}}_{\tau}}\leq\|\widehat{\phi^{T}}\|_{L^{\frac{q^{\prime}}{1+q^{\prime}\varepsilon}}_{\tau}}\|\widehat{\mathcal{K}}_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}}_{\tau}}\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{q}-\varepsilon}

for small
\varepsilon>0
.
From (
7.24
), we have

\displaystyle\|\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(4)}(0,t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T))}\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{q}}.

(7.27)

In view of
a faster decay in
n_{2}
for
j=5
in (
7.7
),
the estimate (
7.27
) trivially holds
for
\widehat{\mathbb{A}}^{(5)}
.
∎

8.
Local well-posedness of Hartree SdNLW

In this section,
we present the proofs of
Theorems
2.7
and
2.9

on local well-posedness
of the renormalized Hartree SdNLW
systems (
2.31
) and (
2.38
)
in the defocusing case and the focusing case, respectively.

\bullet

Defocusing case for
\beta>1
.

We first treat the defocusing case (
2.31
).
By writing (
2.31
) in the Duhamel formulation (for
X
and
Y
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}X&=\Phi_{1}(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})\\
:\!&=S(t)(X_{0},X_{1})-\mathcal{I}\Big(\big(V\ast(Q_{X,Y}+2\mathfrak{R}\,+\!:\!\Psi^{2}\!:)\big)\mathbin{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces
}{{{{\ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.125pt}{-1.75pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}}{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

Remark 8.1
.

As for proving the local well-posedness result stated in Theorem
2.7
,
we do not need to use the
C^{1}_{T}W^{-\frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}
-norm
of the stochastic convolution
\Psi

However, this norm is needed for constructing global-in-time dynamics
and thus we have included it in the definition of
the
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
-norm in (
8.3

The same comment applies to
the first component of the
{\mathcal{Y}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}
-norm defined in (
8.14

&\leq\int_{0}^{T}|M_{\gamma}(Q_{X,Y}+2\mathfrak{R}\,+\!:\!\Psi^{2}\!:)(t^{\prime})|\cdot\|\mathbb{A}(t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{3}_{t}([t^{\prime},T];H^{s_{3}}_{x})}dt^{\prime}\\
&\leq K\|Q_{X,Y}+2\mathfrak{R}\,+\!:\!\Psi^{2}\!:\|_{L^{\gamma-1}_{T}H^{-100}_{x}}^{\gamma-1}\\
&\lesssim T^{\frac{4-\gamma}{3}}K\Big(\|(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}^{2}+K^{2}\Big)^{\gamma-1}.\end{split}

(8.18)

Since
\gamma\leq 3
,
we have a
small power of
T
in (
8.16
), (
8.17
), and (
8.18
).
Furthermore, since
\gamma\geq 2
,

|x|^{\gamma-2}x
is differentiable
with a locally bounded derivative
and thus difference estimates also hold for these extra terms.
Therefore,
proceeding as in the defocusing case,
we can show
that

\vec{\Psi}:=(\Psi_{1},\Psi_{2},\Psi_{3})

is a contraction on the ball
B_{R}\subset Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)

of radius
R\sim\|(X_{0},X_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s_{1}}}+\|(Y_{0},Y_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s_{2}}}+1
.
This proves
Theorem
2.9

in the focusing case.

9.
Invariant Gibbs dynamics

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem
2.1

by applying Bourgain’s invariant measure argument
[
11
,
13
]
.
In Subsection
9.1
,
we first study the truncated dynamics
and establish a long time a priori bound on the solutions (Proposition
9.4
).
In Subsection
9.2
,
we then prove almost sure global well-posedness of the Hartree SdNLW
and invariance of the Hartree Gibbs measure.
Our presentation closely follows those
in
[
92
,
22
,
72
]
,
in particular
[
72
]
, where a renormalization was required on the nonlinearity.
We, however, point out that
a certain part of the argument from
[
72
]
in the two-dimensional setting
can not be applied to the current three-dimensional setting,
where we imposed the paracontrolled structure
for constructing local-in-time solutions.
More precisely, in estimating the difference of two solutions,
the authors in
[
72
]
applied
the product estimates (such as Lemma
3.3
)
to bound the difference of the enhanced data sets
with two different initial data
(and iterated the local-in-time argument).
Such an estimate, however, fails in the three-dimensional setting
due to the lower regularity of the noise.
See Remark
9.10
below
for a further discussion.
We instead establish a stability result on
a large time interval
[0,T]
in a direct manner,
incorporating the paracontrolled structure.
45
45

45

In a preprint
[
18
]
,
Bringmann overcame a similar issue via a different approach,
by establishing a certain stability result of a paracontrolled structure.

See
Proposition
9.7
.

In the following, we only consider the focusing case (
\sigma>0
).
A straightforward modification yields the corresponding result for
the defocusing case.
Furthermore, we restrict our attention
to the non-endpoint case
\beta>2
and assume
\sigma=1

for simplicity.
The same argument applies to the critical case
\beta=2

with
0<\sigma\ll 1
.

In the remaining part of this section,
we fix some notations.
Let
V
be the Bessel potential of order
\beta>2
.
We also fix

A>0
sufficiently large
and
\gamma>0
, satisfying

\max\big(\frac{\beta+1}{\beta-1},2\big)\leq\gamma<3

with
\gamma>2
when
\beta=3
,
such that the focusing Hartree measure

\rho
in (
1.53
) is constructed as the limit of
the truncated Gibbs measures
\rho_{N}

in (
1.50
)
as in Theorem
1.16
.
With these parameters
and
\mu_{0}
as in (
1.20
),
the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}=\rho\otimes\mu_{0}

for the focusing Hartree SdNLW (
2.1
)
is constructed
as the limit of
the truncated Gibbs measures:

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}=\rho_{N}\otimes\mu_{0}

(9.1)

for the truncated focusing Hartree SdNLW (
2.3
);
see Remark
1.11
.

By assumption, the Gaussian field
\vec{\mu}=\mu_{1}\otimes\mu_{0}
in (
1.21
)
and hence the (truncated) Gibbs measures
are independent of (the distribution of) the space-time white noise
\xi
in (
2.1
)
and (
2.3
).
Hence, we can write the probability space
\Omega

as

\displaystyle\Omega=\Omega_{1}\times\Omega_{2}

(9.2)

such that the random Fourier series in (
1.23
) depend only on
\omega_{1}\in\Omega_{1}
,
while the cylindrical Wiener process
W
in (
2.10
)
depends only on
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
.
In view of (
9.2
),
we also write the underlying probability measure
\mathbb{P}
on
\Omega

as
\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{1}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
,
where
\mathbb{P}_{j}
is the marginal probability measure on
\Omega_{j}
,
j=1,2
.

With the decomposition (
9.2
) in mind,
we set

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Psi(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=S(t)\vec{u}_{0}+\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})dW(t^{\prime},\omega_{2}),\\
\vec{\Psi}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=\big(\Psi(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\partial_{t}\Psi(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big),\\
\vphantom{\int}\Psi_{N}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=\pi_{N}\Psi(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\end{split}

(9.3)

for
\vec{u}_{0}=(u_{0},u_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
and
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
,
where
S(t)
is as in (
8.2
).
We may suppress the dependence on
t
and
\omega_{2}

and write
\Psi(\vec{u}_{0})
, etc.

In the remaining part of this section,
we fix

\frac{1}{4}<s_{1}<\frac{1}{2}<s_{2}<1
and
-\frac{1}{2}<s_{3}<0
,
satisfying (
2.33
),
as in (the proof of) Theorem
2.9

on the local well-posedness
of the focusing Hartree SdNLW system (
2.38
).

9.1.
On the truncated dynamics

In this subsection, we
study the truncated focusing Hartree SdNLW (
2.3
):

\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}^{2}&u_{N}+\partial_{t}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)u_{N}\\
&-\sigma\pi_{N}\big((V\ast:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)\pi_{N}u_{N}\big)+M_{\gamma}(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)\pi_{N}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\xi,\end{split}

(9.4)

where

:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,=(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}

and
M_{\gamma}
is as in (
2.2
).
While local well-posedness of the truncated equation (
9.4
)
follows from a small modification of the proof of Theorem
2.9
,
we present a simple argument
to prove local well-posedness of (
9.4
)
(Lemma
9.1
).
Then, we prove almost sure global well-posedness
of the truncated equation (
9.4
) and
invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

in (
9.1
) (Lemma
9.3
).

Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
let

\vec{u}_{0}=(u_{0},u_{1})

be a pair of random distributions such that

\Law((u_{0},u_{1}))=\vec{\rho}_{N}=\rho_{N}\otimes\mu_{0}

defined in (
9.1
).
Let
u_{N}
be a solution
to the truncated equation (
9.4
) with
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}
.
With

:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,=(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}
,
we write (
9.4
)
as

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}^{2}u_{N}+\partial_{t}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)u_{N}-\sigma\pi_{N}\big((V\ast((\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}))\pi_{N}u_{N}\big)\\
\quad+M_{\gamma}((\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N})\pi_{N}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\xi,\\
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}.\end{cases}

(9.5)

The
dynamics of (
9.5
)
is decoupled into the
high frequency part
\{|n|>N\}

and the low frequency part
\{|n|\leq N\}
.
The high frequency part of the dynamics (
9.5
) is given by

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}^{2}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}+\partial_{t}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}^{\perp}\xi\end{aligned}\\
(\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N},\partial_{t}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\vec{u}_{0},\end{cases}

(9.6)

where

\pi_{N}^{\perp}=\text{Id}-\pi_{N}
,
and thus
the solution
\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}
to (
9.6
) is given by

\displaystyle\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\Psi(\vec{u}_{0}).

(9.7)

With
v_{N}=\pi_{N}u_{N}
,
the low frequency part of the dynamics (
9.5
) is given by

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}^{2}v_{N}+\partial_{t}v_{N}+(1-\Delta)v_{N}-\sigma\pi_{N}\big((V\ast((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}))\pi_{N}v_{N}\big)\\
\quad+M_{\gamma}((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N})\pi_{N}v_{N}=\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}\xi,\\
(v_{N},\partial_{t}v_{N})|_{t=0}=\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}.\end{cases}

(9.8)

Note that we kept
\pi_{N}
in several places to emphasize that
(
9.8
) depends only on finite many frequencies
\{|n|\leq N\}
.
By writing (
9.8
)
in the Duhamel formulation,
we have

\displaystyle v_{N}(t)

\displaystyle=\pi_{N}S(t)\vec{u}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}+\Psi_{N}(t;0),

(9.9)

where the truncated nonlinearity
\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})
is given by

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})=\sigma\pi_{N}\big((V\ast((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}))\pi_{N}v_{N}\big)-M_{\gamma}((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N})\pi_{N}v_{N}

and
\Psi_{N}(t;0)=\pi_{N}\Psi_{N}(t;0)
is as in (
9.3
) with
\vec{u}_{0}=0
.
Recall from Lemma
4.1

that
\Psi_{N}(t;0)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.
By viewing
\Psi_{N}(t;0)
in (
9.9
) as a perturbation,
it suffices to study
the following damped NLW with a deterministic perturbation:

\displaystyle v_{N}(t)

\displaystyle=\pi_{N}S(t)(v_{0},v_{1})+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}+F,

(9.10)

where
(v_{0},v_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
,
\sigma_{N}
is as in (
1.26
), and

F\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
is a given deterministic function.

Lemma 9.1
.

Let
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Given any

(v_{0},v_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
and
F\in C([0,1];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
with

\|(v_{0},v_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}\leq R\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|F\|_{C^{1}([0,1];H^{1})}\leq K

for some
R,K\geq 1
,
there exist
\tau=\tau(R,K,N)>0
and a unique solution
v_{N}
to (
9.10
) on
[0,\tau]
,
satisfying the bound:

\|v_{N}\|_{X^{1}(\tau)}\lesssim R+K,

where
X^{1}(\tau)
is as in (
2.32
).
Moreover, the solution
v_{N}
is unique
in
X^{1}(\tau)
.

While the local existence time depends on
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
Lemma
9.1
suffices for our purpose.

Proof.

Let
\Phi_{N}(v_{N})
denote the right-hand side of (
9.10
).
Let
0<\tau\leq 1
.
Then, from (
2.8
), (
8.8
), and Sobolev’s inequality
with (
2.2
), we have

\displaystyle\|

\displaystyle\Phi_{N}(v_{N})\|_{X^{1}(\tau)}

\displaystyle\lesssim\|(v_{0},v_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}+\tau\big\|V\ast\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)\big\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}L^{3}_{x}}\|v_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}L^{6}_{x}}

\displaystyle\quad+\tau\big\|M_{\gamma}\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)\big\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}}\|v_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}L^{2}_{x}}+\|F\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}H^{1}_{x}}

\displaystyle\lesssim R+\tau\Big(\|v_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}H^{1}_{x}}^{2(\gamma-1)}+\sigma_{N}^{\gamma-1}\Big)\|v_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}H^{1}_{x}}+K

\displaystyle\lesssim R+K

for any
v_{N}\in X^{1}(\tau)
with
\|v_{N}\|_{X^{1}(\tau)}\leq C_{0}(R+K)
,
where the last step holds by choosing

\tau=\tau(R,K,N)>0

sufficiently small.
A difference estimate also follows in a similar manner since
\gamma\geq 2
.
Hence, we conclude that

\Phi_{N}
is a contraction on the ball
B_{C_{0}(R+K)}\subset X^{1}(\tau)
for some
C_{0}>0
.
At this point, the uniqueness holds only in the ball

B_{C_{0}(R+K)}
but by a standard continuity argument, we can extend the uniqueness to hold in the entire
X^{1}(\tau)
. We omit details.
∎

Remark 9.2
.

(i) From the proof, we see that

\tau=\tau(R,K,N)\sim(R+K+N)^{-\theta}

for some
\theta>0
.
In particular, the local existence time
\tau
depends on
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

(ii)
Note that the uniqueness statement
for
v_{N}
in Lemma
9.1
is unconditional,
namely, the uniqueness of the solution
v_{N}
holds in the entire class

X^{1}(\tau)
.
Then, from (
9.7
) and
the unconditional uniqueness of the solution
v_{N}=v_{N}(\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0})
to (
9.8
),
we obtain the
unique
representation of
u_{N}
:

\displaystyle u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\immediate\makebox[3.81412pt][c]{\hbox to3.81412pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0})+\pi_{N}v_{N}(\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}).

(9.11)

This uniqueness statement
for
u_{N}
plays an important role in Proposition
9.4

and Lemma
9.8
.
See Remarks
9.5
and
9.9
below.

Before proceeding further, let us introduce some notations.
Given the cylindrical Wiener process
W
in (
2.10
),
by possibly enlarging the probability space
\Omega_{2}
,
there exists a family of translations
\tau_{t_{0}}:\Omega_{2}\to\Omega_{2}
such that

\displaystyle W(t,\tau_{t_{0}}(\omega_{2}))=W(t+t_{0},\omega_{2})-W(t_{0},\omega_{2})

(9.12)

for
t,t_{0}\geq 0
and
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
.
Denote by
\Phi^{N}(t)
the stochastic flow map
to the truncated equation (
9.4
)
given in Lemma
9.1

(which is not necessarily global at this point).
Namely,

\vec{u}_{N}(t)=\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

is the solution
to (
9.4
) with

\vec{u}_{N}|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}
, satisfying
\Law(\vec{u}_{0})=\vec{\rho}_{N}
,
and the noise
\xi(\omega_{2})
.
We now
extend
\Phi^{N}(t)
as

\displaystyle\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\big(\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\tau_{t}(\omega_{2})\big).

(9.13)

Note that
by the uniqueness of the solution to (
9.4
),
we have

\displaystyle\Phi^{N}(t_{1}+t_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\Phi^{N}(t_{2})\big(\Phi^{N}(t_{1})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\tau_{t_{1}}(\omega_{2})\big)=\Phi^{N}(t_{2})\big(\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t_{1})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)

(9.14)

for
t_{1},t_{2}\geq 0

as long as the flow is well defined.

Next, by exploiting invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
,
we construct global-in-time solutions
to (
9.4
) almost surely with respect to the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
9.1
).

Lemma 9.3
.

Let
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then, the truncated focusing Hartree SdNLW (
9.4
) is almost surely globally well-posed
with respect to the random initial data distributed
by the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
9.1
).
Furthermore,
\vec{\rho}_{N}
is invariant under the resulting dynamics.

Proof.

We first discuss the (formal) invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

under the truncated dynamics (
9.4
).
Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
, let
\pi_{N}^{\perp}=\text{Id}-\pi_{N}
.
We define
the marginal probability measures

\vec{\mu}_{N}
and
\vec{\mu}_{N}^{\perp}

on
\pi_{N}\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})

and
\pi_{N}^{\perp}\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
, respectively,
as
the induced probability measures
under the following maps:

\omega_{1}\in\Omega_{1}\longmapsto(\pi_{N}u^{\omega_{1}},\pi_{N}v^{\omega_{1}})

for

\vec{\mu}_{N}

and

\omega_{1}\in\Omega_{1}\longmapsto(\pi_{N}^{\perp}u^{\omega_{1}},\pi_{N}^{\perp}v^{\omega_{1}})

for
\vec{\mu}_{N}^{\perp}
,
where

u^{\omega_{1}}
and
v^{\omega_{1}}
are as in (
1.23
)
with
\omega
replaced by
\omega_{1}
in view of the decomposition (
9.2
).
Then, we have

\displaystyle\vec{\mu}=\vec{\mu}_{N}\otimes\vec{\mu}_{N}^{\perp}.

(9.15)

From
(
9.1
) with
(
1.21
),
(
1.50
), and (
9.15
),
we then have

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}=\vec{\nu}_{N}\otimes\vec{\mu}_{N}^{\perp},

(9.16)

where
\vec{\nu}_{N}
is given by

\displaystyle d\vec{\nu}_{N}=\widehat{Z}_{N}^{-1}e^{\mathcal{R}_{N}(u)}d\vec{\mu}_{N}

(9.17)

with the density
\mathcal{R}_{N}
as in (
1.49
).

By writing
u_{N}
as
u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}+\pi_{N}u_{N}
,
we see that
the high frequency part

\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\Psi(\vec{u}_{0})

satisfies the linear dynamics (
9.6
).
It is easy to check that the Gaussian measure
\vec{\mu}_{N}^{\perp}

is invariant under the dynamics of (
9.6
),
say, by studying (
9.6
) for each frequency
|n|>N

on the Fourier side.
The low frequency part
\pi_{N}u_{N}
satisfies
(
9.8
).
By writing (
9.8
) in the Ito formulation
with
(u_{N}^{1},u_{N}^{2})=(\pi_{N}u_{N},\partial_{t}\pi_{N}u_{N})
,
it is easy to see that
the generator
\mathcal{L}^{N}
for (
9.8
)
can be written as
\mathcal{L}^{N}=\mathcal{L}^{N}_{1}+\mathcal{L}^{N}_{2}
,
where
\mathcal{L}^{N}_{1}
denotes the generator
for the undamped NLW with the truncated nonlinearity:

\displaystyle\begin{split}d\begin{pmatrix}u_{N}^{1}\\
u_{N}^{2}\end{pmatrix}+\Bigg\{\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1-\Delta&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_{N}^{1}\\
u_{N}^{2}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
-\mathcal{N}_{N}(\pi_{N}u_{N}^{1})\end{pmatrix}\Bigg\}dt=0\end{split}

(9.18)

and
\mathcal{L}^{N}_{2}
denotes the generator
for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
(for the second component
u_{N}^{2}
):

\displaystyle\begin{split}d\begin{pmatrix}u_{N}^{1}\\
u_{N}^{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
-u_{N}^{2}dt+\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}dW\end{pmatrix}.\end{split}

(9.19)

By recalling that the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
preserves the standard Gaussian measure,
we conclude that
\vec{\nu}_{N}
is invariant under the linear dynamics (
9.19
)
since
the measure
\vec{\nu}_{N}
is nothing but the white noise measure
(projected onto the low frequencies
\{|n|\leq N\}
)
on the second component
u_{N}^{2}
.
As for (
9.18
), we note that it is a Hamiltonian equation with the Hamiltonian:

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}^{\sharp}_{N}(u_{N}^{1},u_{N}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}|\langle\nabla\rangle u_{N}^{1}|^{2}dx+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(u_{N}^{2})^{2}dx-\mathcal{R}_{N}(u^{1}_{N}),

where
\mathcal{R}_{N}
is as in (
1.49
) (with
\sigma=1
).
Then, from the conservation of the Hamiltonian

\mathcal{E}^{\sharp}_{N}(u_{N}^{1},u_{N}^{2})
and Liouville’s theorem
(on the finite-dimensional phase space
\pi_{N}\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
),
we conclude that
\vec{\nu}_{N}
in (
9.17
) is invariant under the dynamics of (
9.18
).
Therefore, we conclude that

(\mathcal{L}^{N})^{*}\vec{\nu}_{N}=(\mathcal{L}^{N}_{1})^{*}\vec{\nu}_{N}+(\mathcal{L}^{N}_{2})^{*}\vec{\nu}_{N}=0,

where

(\mathcal{L}^{N})^{\ast}
denotes the the adjoint of the infinitesimal
generator
\mathcal{L}^{N}=\mathcal{L}^{N}_{1}+\mathcal{L}^{N}_{2}

for (
9.8
).
This shows invariance of
\vec{\nu}_{N}
under (
9.8
).

Therefore, from (
9.16
)
and the invariance of
\vec{\mu}^{\perp}_{N}
and
\vec{\nu}_{N}

under (
9.6
) and (
9.8
), respectively, we conclude that the truncated Gibbs measure

\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
9.1
)
is
formally
invariant
under the dynamics of
the truncated focusing Hartree SdNLW
(
9.4
).
Here, by the formal invariance,
we mean that the
\vec{\rho}_{N}
-measure of a measurable set
is preserved under the truncated dynamics (
9.4
) as long as the flow is well defined.
In view of the translation invariance of the law
of the Brownian motions
\{B_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}

in (
2.10
),
we also conclude formal invariance of

\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

under the extended stochastic flow map
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)
defined in (
9.13
).

Next, by exploiting this formal invariance of
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
,
we establish almost sure global well-posedness of
(
9.4
).
By arguing as in
[
11
,
25
,
6
]
,
it suffices to show “almost” almost sure global existence.
Namely, we prove that,
given any
T\geq 1
and
\kappa>0
,
there exists
\Sigma_{T,\kappa}\subset\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}
such that

\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma_{T,\kappa}^{c})<\kappa
and for any
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{T,\kappa}
,
there exists a solution
u_{N}
to (
9.4
)
on the time interval
[0,T]
.

We follow the ideas from
[
11
,
72
]
.
Given
T\geq 1
and
\kappa>0
,
let

\displaystyle K\sim c_{N}\bigg(\log\frac{T}{\kappa}+\log C_{N}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}

(9.20)

for some suitable
c_{N},C_{N}>0
.
Then,
with
\tau=\tau(K,K,N)>0
as in Lemma
9.1

(see also Remark
9.2
),
we set

\displaystyle\Sigma_{T,\kappa}=\bigcap_{j=0}^{[T/\tau]}\Big\{

\displaystyle(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}:\|\Phi^{N}(j\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}\leq K,

\displaystyle\|\Psi_{N}(\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(j\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau,x}}\leq K\Big\}.

By the definition of
\Sigma_{T,\kappa}

and the local well-posedness argument (Lemma
9.1
),
we see that, given any

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{T,\kappa}
, the corresponding solution
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})
to (
9.4
) exists on
[0,T]
.

By Bernstein’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\|\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}

\displaystyle\lesssim N^{\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon}\|\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}},

\displaystyle\|\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau,x}}

\displaystyle\lesssim N^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}\|\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau}W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}.

Then, from the (formal) invariance of
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

under the extended stochastic flow map
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)
in (
9.13
),
Remark
9.2
, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
with Theorem
1.16

(in particular, the bound (
1.51
)),
Lemma
4.1
,
and (
9.20
), we have

\displaystyle\rho_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma_{T,\kappa}^{c})

\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{T}{\tau}\bigg\{\rho_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}):\|\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}>K\big)

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXX}+\rho_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}):\|\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau,x}}>K\big)\bigg\}

\displaystyle\leq C_{N}TK^{\theta}\bigg\{\mu\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}):\|\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}>K\big)

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}+\mu\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}):\|\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{L^{\infty}_{\tau,x}}>K\big)\bigg\}^{\frac{1}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq C_{N}T\cdot Ce^{-c^{\prime}_{N}K^{2}}\ll\kappa.

This proves the desired
“almost” almost sure global existence, and thus almost sure global well-posedness
of the truncated focusing Hartree SdNLW (
9.4
).
Since the dynamics is now globally well defined
almost surely with respect to
\vec{\rho}_{N}
,
we conclude invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

from the formal invariance of
\vec{\rho}_{N}
discussed above.
∎

We now establish a long time a priori bound on
the solutions to the truncated equation (
9.4
).
We emphasize that the following growth bound (
9.22
) with (
9.21
) is independent of
N
,
which is contrast to all earlier results of this section.

Proposition 9.4
.

Let

i\in\mathbb{N}
and
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then,
there exists a
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
-measurable set

\Sigma^{i}_{N}\subset\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}
such that

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2})\setminus\Sigma^{i}_{N}\big)\leq 2^{-i}.

(9.21)

Moreover,
there exists
C>0
such that
for any
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma^{i}_{N}
and
t\geq 0
,
we have

\displaystyle\big\|\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big\|_{\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\leq C(i+\log(1+t)).

(9.22)

Proof.

We follow the argument in
[
72
]
.
Given
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}

\displaystyle\Psi_{N}=\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

(9.23)

and

are defined as above.
Then, by repeating
the proof of Theorem
2.9

(see (
8.9
) - (
8.11
) and (
8.16
) - (
8.18
))
with the uniform boundedness of
\pi_{N}
,

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in B^{i,j}_{N}(D)
(see (
9.25
)) and (
9.28
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|(X_{N},&Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}\\
&\lesssim\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}K\Big(\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}^{3}+K^{3}\Big)\\
&\quad+\tau^{\frac{4-\gamma}{3}}\Big(\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}+K\Big)^{2\gamma-1}\\
&\lesssim\big(D(i+j)\big)^{1-\frac{2}{3}\theta}\Big(\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}^{3}+\big(D(i+j)\big)^{3}\Big)\\
&\quad+\big(D(i+j)\big)^{-\frac{4-\gamma}{3}\theta}\Big(\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}+\big(D(i+j)\big)\Big)^{2\gamma-1},\end{split}

(9.31)

where

K=\|\Xi(\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))\|_{\mathcal{Y}^{\varepsilon}_{1}}+1
.
Then, by taking sufficiently large
\theta\gg 1

and
D\gg 1
(independent of
i,j,N\in\mathbb{N}
),
a standard
continuity argument with (
9.31
) yields

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(\tau)}\leq 1.\end{split}

(9.32)

Then, (
9.27
) follows
from the decomposition (
9.29
) with the bounds
(
9.25
)
and
(
9.32
).

Next, we set

\displaystyle\Sigma^{i,j}_{N}=\bigcap_{\ell=0}^{[2^{j}/\tau]}\big(\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(\ell\tau)\big)^{-1}\big(B^{i,j}_{N}(D)\big),

(9.33)

where
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)
is the extended stochastic flow map
in (
9.13
).
Then, from the invariance of
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

under
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)
(from the proof of Lemma
9.3
), (
9.26
), and (
9.28
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes&\,\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega)\setminus\Sigma^{i,j}_{N}\big)\\
&\leq C\frac{2^{j}}{\tau}\cdot\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big((\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega)\setminus B^{i,j}_{N}(D)\big)\\
&\leq C2^{j}D^{\theta}(i+j)^{\theta}\exp\big(-cD(i+j)\big)\\
&\leq 2^{-(i+j)},\end{split}

(9.34)

uniformly in
i,j,N\in\mathbb{N}
,
provided that
D\gg 1
.
Moreover, from (
9.33
) and (
9.27
)
with the flow property (
9.14
), we have

\displaystyle\|\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\leq D(i+j+1)

(9.35)

for
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma^{i,j}_{N}
and
0\leq t\leq 2^{j}
.

Finally, we set

\displaystyle\Sigma^{i}_{N}=\bigcap_{j=1}^{\infty}\Sigma^{i,j}_{N}.

(9.36)

Then, (
9.21
)
follows from (
9.34
).
The growth bound
(
9.22
) follows from
(
9.35
).
∎

Remark 9.5
.

(i) In the proof of Proposition
9.4
,
we used two different decompositions
(
9.11
)
and (
9.29
)
for the solution
u_{N}
to the truncated equation (
9.4
).
The former was used to obtain (
9.34
),
while the latter was used to obtain (
9.35
).
The unconditional uniqueness statement
for
u_{N}
in Remark
9.2

was essential to conclude that
these solutions given by the two different decompositions coincide.

(ii)
Note that
the power in the growth bound (
9.22
)
comes from the fact that
the enhanced data set

\Xi(\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))
in (
9.24
)
belongs to
\mathcal{H}_{\leq 2}

in the focusing case.
In the defocusing case,
the associated enhanced data set
belongs to
\mathcal{H}_{\leq 3}

and thus we need to replace the right-hand side of (
9.22
)
by

C(i+\log(1+t))^{\frac{3}{2}}
.

We conclude this subsection by stating a corollary to Proposition
9.4
.

Corollary 9.6
.

Given
i\in\mathbb{N}
and
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
let
\Sigma_{N}^{i}
be as in Proposition
9.4
.
Fix
T\gg 1

and let
j
be the smallest integer such that
2^{j}\geq T

and
\tau>0
be as in (
9.28
).
Then, there exists
C(i,T)>0
such that

\displaystyle\sup_{(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{N}^{i}}\|V*:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\|_{\ell^{\infty}_{k}L^{3}([k\tau,(k+1)\tau];H^{-s_{1}+s_{2}+\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\beta-1-\varepsilon,\infty})}\leq C(i,T),

(9.37)

\displaystyle\sup_{(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{N}^{i}}\|:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\|_{\ell^{\infty}_{k}L^{3}([k\tau,(k+1)\tau];H^{-100})}\leq C(i,T),

(9.38)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
where

V
is the Bessel potential of order
\beta\geq 2

and
u_{N}=\Phi_{1}^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
is as in (
9.29
),
denoting the global-in-time solution to the truncated Hartree SdNLW (
9.4
).

Proof.

We only prove the first bound (
9.37
), since the second bound
(
9.38
) follows from (
9.37
) and Sobolev’s inequality.
Given

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{N}^{i}
,
it follows from
(
9.36
) and (
9.33
) that

\displaystyle\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\big(\Phi^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\tau_{k\tau}(\omega_{2})\big)\in B^{i,j}_{N}(D)

for any
k=0,1,\dots,\big[\frac{2^{j}}{\tau}\big]
,
where
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}
is as in (
9.13
).

Now, consider the
truncated dynamics
(
9.4
) on
the time interval
[k\tau,(k+1)\tau]

with
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=k\tau}=\Phi^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

and the noise parameter
\tau_{k\tau}(\omega_{2})
.
Let
\mathfrak{t}=t-k\tau
denote the shifted time.
Then, it suffices to study the system (
9.30
)
for
0\leq\mathfrak{t}\leq\tau
,
where the enhanced data set

\Xi(\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))
in (
9.24
)
is based on

\Psi_{N}
given by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Psi_{N}(\mathfrak{t})&=\Psi_{N}\big(\mathfrak{t};\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)\\
&=\pi_{N}S(\mathfrak{t})\big(\Phi^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)+\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}\int_{0}^{\mathfrak{t}}\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{t}-t^{\prime})dW(t^{\prime},\tau_{k\tau}(\omega_{2}))\end{split}

(9.39)

and

Q_{X_{N},Y_{N}}
is as in
(
2.23
) with
\Psi
replaced by

\Psi_{N}
in (
9.39
).
For clarity, let us denote the solution to (
9.30
)
on
[k\tau,(k+1)\tau]

by
(X_{N}^{(k)},Y_{N}^{(k)},\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{(k)})
.
Arguing
as in the proof of Proposition
9.4
,
we obtain (by expressing in terms of the original time
t=\mathfrak{t}+k\tau
)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|(X_{N}^{(k)},Y_{N}^{(k)},\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{(k)})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}([k\tau,(k+1)\tau])}\leq 1,\end{split}

(9.40)

where, with a slight abuse of notation,
we used
Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(I)

to denote
the
Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}
-norm restricted to a given time interval
I
.
Then,
by writing

\displaystyle V*:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,=V*(Q_{X_{N}^{(k)},Y_{N}^{(k)}}+2\mathfrak{R}_{N}^{(k)}+:\!\Psi_{N}^{2}\!:),

we obtain from (
9.40
) and (
8.6
) with (
9.25
)
and the regularity ranges
\frac{1}{4}<s_{1}<\frac{1}{2}<s_{2}<1
and
-\frac{1}{2}<s_{3}<0

from Theorem
2.9

that

\displaystyle\|V*:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\|_{L^{3}([k\tau,(k+1)\tau];H^{-s_{1}+s_{2}+\frac{1}{2}}+W^{\beta-1-\varepsilon,\infty})}\leq C(i,j),

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
,

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{N}^{i}
, and

k=0,1,\dots,\big[\frac{2^{j}}{\tau}\big]
.
This proves (
9.37
).
∎

9.2.
Proof of Theorem
2.1

In this subsection, by an approximation argument,
we first prove almost sure global well-posedness
of the focusing Hartree SdNLW (
2.1
).
Given
i\in\mathbb{N}
, define
a set
\Sigma^{i}
by

\displaystyle\Sigma^{i}=\limsup_{N\to\infty}\Sigma^{i}_{N}=\bigcap_{N=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{M=N}^{\infty}\Sigma^{i}_{M}.

(9.41)

Then, from
(
9.41
), Theorem
1.16
,
and (
9.21
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma^{i})&=\lim_{N\to\infty}\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\bigg(\bigcup_{M=N}^{\infty}\Sigma^{i}_{M}\bigg)\\
&\geq\limsup_{N\to\infty}\,\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma^{i}_{N})=\limsup_{N\to\infty}\,\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma^{i}_{N})\\
&\geq 1-2^{-i}.\end{split}

Hence, by setting

\displaystyle\Sigma=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma^{i},

(9.42)

we obtain

\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma)=1.

In view of
Lemma
9.3
,
without loss of generality,
we assume that given any
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma
,
there exists the global-in-time solution
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})
to (
9.4
)
with
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}

and the noise parameter
\omega_{2}

(i.e. with the external forcing
\xi(\omega_{2})
).

Fix
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma
.
Then, it follows from
(
9.42
), (
9.41
), (
9.36
), and (
9.33
)
that
there exist
i\in\mathbb{N}
and an increasing sequence
\{N_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
such that

\displaystyle(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma^{i}_{N_{k}}=\bigcap_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigcap_{\ell=0}^{[2^{j}/\tau]}\big(\widehat{\Phi}^{N_{k}}(\ell\tau)\big)^{-1}(B^{i,j}_{N_{k}}(D))

(9.43)

for any
k\in\mathbb{N}
,
where
\tau=\tau(i,j,D)>0
is as in (
9.28
).

In the next proposition,
we prove convergence of
the solutions
\{\Phi^{N_{k}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}

along this particular subsequence
N_{k}=N_{k}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
.
In Corollary
9.12
,
we establish convergence of the entire sequence

\{\Phi^{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.
See also Remark
9.11
.

Proposition 9.7
.

Let
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma
,
i\in\mathbb{N}
, and
\{N_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}

be as above.
Then,

\{\Phi^{N_{k}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
is a Cauchy sequence
in
C(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

endowed with the
compact-open topology
(
in time
)
.

Before proceeding to the proof of
Proposition
9.7
,
we first establish a
growth bound
for the solution

(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})
to the truncated system (
9.30
)
with
\Psi_{N}=\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

on a given (large) time interval

.

Suppose that we have

(

)

.

With

\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}}{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

Remark 9.9
.

In the proof of Lemma
9.8
,
we crucially used the
unconditional uniqueness of
the solution
u_{N}
to the truncated equation (
9.4
).
More precisely,
in the proof of Lemma
9.8
,
we studied the equation (
9.46
)
on a large time interval
[0,T]
,
where we used the representation

\displaystyle u_{N}(t)=\Psi_{N}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+X_{N}(t)+Y_{N}(t).

(9.50)

On the other hand, we used Corollary
9.6

for the bound on
V*\!:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:

whose proof is based on
studying
the system (
9.30
)
on the subinterval
[k\tau,(k+1)\tau]

with (
9.39
).
In this case, the enhanced data set
on each subinterval
[k\tau,(k+1)\tau]

was constructed from

\Psi_{N}(\mathfrak{t})=\Psi_{N}\big(\mathfrak{t};\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)
,
where
\mathfrak{t}=t-k\tau
.
Namely, we used the representation

\displaystyle u_{N}(t)=\Psi_{N}\big(t-k\tau;\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(k\tau)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)+X^{(k)}_{N}(t-k\tau)+Y^{(k)}_{N}(t-k\tau)

(9.51)

for
t\in[k\tau,(k+1)\tau]
.
The unconditional uniqueness of
u_{N}

guarantees that the two representations
(
9.50
) and (
9.51
)
agree, thus allowing us to use
Corollary
9.6

in the proof of Lemma
9.8
.
This in turn allowed us to
express the
Y_{N}
-equation in (
9.46
)
linearly in
Y_{N}
,
which was crucial in applying
the discrete Gronwall inequality.

0-
and
1-
, respectively,
and thus there is no issue in making sense of the resonant product in (
9.52
).

We are now ready to prove
Proposition
9.7
.

Proof of
Proposition
9.7
.

Fix
T\gg 1
.
We prove
that
\{\Phi^{N_{k}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
is a Cauchy sequence
in
C([0,T];\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.

Given
\lambda=\lambda(i,T)\gg 1
(to be determined later),
we define

\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)
by

\displaystyle\|(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}=\|(e^{-\lambda t}X,e^{-\lambda t}Y,e^{-\lambda t}\mathfrak{R})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}.

(9.53)

For notational simplicity,
we also set
Z_{N}=(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})

and
\Xi_{N}=\Xi(\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))
,
where
\Xi(\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))
denotes
the enhanced data set defined in (
9.24
).
We consider the truncated system (
9.30
)
on
[0,T]
with
\Psi_{N}=\Psi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

to study the difference
e^{-\lambda t}(Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}})(t)
.

Given
T\gg 1
,
let
j=j(T)
be the smallest integer such that
2^{j}\geq T
.
Recalling that

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma^{i}_{N_{k}}
,
k\in\mathbb{N}
,
it follows from (
9.25
) that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\sup_{\ell=0,1,\dots,j}\|\Xi_{N_{k}}\|_{\mathcal{Y}^{\varepsilon}_{2^{\ell}}}&\leq K=D(i+j),\\
\sup_{\ell=0,1,\dots,j}\|\Xi_{N_{k_{1}}}-\Xi_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Y}^{\varepsilon}_{2^{\ell}}}&\leq N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta}D(i+j)\end{split}

(9.54)

for any
k_{2}\geq k_{1}\geq 1
.
We first estimate

e^{-\lambda t}(X_{N_{k_{1}}}-X_{N_{k_{2}}})(t)
.
Using the Duhamel formulation of (
9.30
),
we have

\displaystyle e^{-\lambda t}X_{N_{k_{1}}}(t)-e^{-\lambda t}X_{N_{k_{2}}}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{1}(t)+e^{-\lambda t}\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}(t)+e^{-\lambda t}\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{3}(t),

(9.55)

where (i)
\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{1}
contains
one of the differences

X_{N_{k_{1}}}-X_{N_{k_{2}}}
,

Y_{N_{k_{1}}}-Y_{N_{k_{2}}}
,
or
\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{1}}}-\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{2}}}
,
(ii)
\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}
contains
the difference
\Psi_{N_{k_{1}}}-\Psi_{N_{k_{2}}}

or

:\!\Psi_{N_{k_{1}}}^{2}\!:-:\!\Psi_{N_{k_{2}}}^{2}\!:
,
and (iii)

\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{3}
contains the terms
with the high frequency projection
\pi_{N_{k_{2}}}-\pi_{N_{k_{1}}}

onto the frequencies
\{N_{k_{1}}<|n|\leq N_{k_{2}}\}
,
which allows us to gain
a small negative power of
N_{k_{1}}

by losing a small amount of regularity.

Proceeding as in (
8.9
)
and (
8.16
)
and then applying Lemma
9.8

and (
9.54
),
we can estimate the last two terms
on the right-hand side of (
9.55
)
as

\displaystyle\begin{split}e^{-\lambda t}\|\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}(t)+\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{3}(t)\|_{H^{s_{1}}}&\leq C(T)\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{2}\|Z_{N_{k_{j}}}\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}^{2}+K^{2}\Big)^{2(\gamma-1)}\\
&\quad\times\Big(\|\Xi_{N_{k_{1}}}-\Xi_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Y}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}+N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta_{0}}K\Big)\\
&\leq C(i,T)N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta_{1}}\end{split}

(9.56)

for any
0\leq t\leq T
and some small
\delta_{0},\delta_{1}>0
.
In order to estimate the first term on the right-hand side of (
9.55
),
we use the following bound:

\displaystyle e^{-\lambda t}\|e^{\lambda t^{\prime}}\|_{L^{q}_{t^{\prime}}([0,t])}\lesssim\lambda^{-\frac{1}{q}}.

(9.57)

Proceeding as above with (
9.53
), (
9.54
), and (
9.57
)
and noting that
K=K(i,j)=K(i,T)
, we have,
for some finite
q\geq 1
,

\displaystyle\begin{split}e^{-\lambda t}\|\hskip 0.56905pt\text{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{1}(t)\|_{H^{s_{1}}}&\leq C(T)e^{-\lambda t}\|e^{\lambda t^{\prime}}\|_{L^{q}_{t^{\prime}}([0,t])}K^{2}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{2}\|Z_{N_{k_{j}}}\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}+K\Big)^{2\gamma-3}\\
&\quad\times\|Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}\\
&\leq C(i,T)\lambda^{-\frac{1}{q}}\|Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}\\
&\leq\frac{1}{10}\|Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}\end{split}

(9.58)

for any
0\leq t\leq T
,
where the last inequality follows from choosing

\lambda=\lambda(i,T)
sufficiently large.
Hence, from (
9.55
), (
9.56
), and (
9.58
),
we obtain

\displaystyle\|e^{-\lambda t}(X_{N_{k_{1}}}-X_{N_{k_{2}}})\|_{X^{s_{1}}(T)}\leq C(i,T)N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta_{1}}+\frac{1}{10}\|Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}.

(9.59)

A similar computation yields

\displaystyle\|e^{-\lambda t}(Y_{N_{k_{1}}}-Y_{N_{k_{2}}})\|_{X^{s_{2}}(T)}\leq C(i,T)N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta_{1}}+\frac{1}{10}\|Z_{N_{k_{1}}}-Z_{N_{k_{2}}}\|_{\mathcal{Z}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}_{\lambda}(T)}.

(9.60)

It remains to estimate
e^{-\lambda t}(\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{1}}}-\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{2}}})(t)
.
Once again, using (
9.30
),
we have

\displaystyle e^{-\lambda t}\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{1}}}(t)-e^{-\lambda t}\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{2}}}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{1}(t)+e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{2}(t)+e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{3}(t),

(9.61)

where (i)
\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{1}
contains
one of the differences

X_{N_{k_{1}}}-X_{N_{k_{2}}}
,

Y_{N_{k_{1}}}-Y_{N_{k_{2}}}
,
or
\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{1}}}-\mathfrak{R}_{N_{k_{2}}}
,
(ii)
\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{2}
contains
the difference of one of the terms in
the enhanced data set
\Xi_{N_{k_{j}}}
,
j=1,2
,
and (iii)
\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{3}
contains the terms
with the high frequency projection
\pi_{N_{k_{2}}}-\pi_{N_{k_{1}}}

onto the frequencies
\{N_{k_{1}}<|n|\leq N_{k_{2}}\}
,
allowing us to gain
a small negative power of
N_{k_{1}}

by losing a small amount of regularity.

Proceeding as in (
8.11
)
and (
8.18
)
and then applying Lemma
9.8
,
we can estimate the last two term
on the right-hand side of (
9.61
)
as

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{2}+e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{3}\|_{L^{3}_{T}H^{s_{3}}_{x}}&\leq C(i,T)N_{k_{1}}^{-\delta_{1}}\end{split}

(9.62)

for any
0\leq t\leq T
and some small
\delta_{1}>0
.
As for the first term on the right-hand side of (
9.61
),
let us first estimate the contribution from
the terms involving

\widetilde{\mathfrak{I}}_{\mathbin{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

Finally, we show invariance of the focusing Hartree Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}
in (
1.53
)
for the limiting process
\vec{u}=(u,\partial_{t}u)
.

and

.
It follows from (

,
the strong convergence of

(Theorem

),

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}_{\omega_{2}}\big[F(\Phi(t)(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}},\omega_{2}))\big]d\vec{\rho}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})

\displaystyle=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\mathbb{E}_{\omega_{2}}\big[F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}},\omega_{2}))\big]d\vec{\rho}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})

\displaystyle=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\mathbb{E}_{\omega_{2}}\big[F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}},\omega_{2}))\big]d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})

\displaystyle=\lim_{N\to\infty}\int F(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})

\displaystyle=\int F(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}})d\vec{\rho}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\omega_{1}}).

.

.

Appendix A
On the parabolic stochastic quantization
of the focusing Hartree Gibbs measure

In this section,
we consider the parabolic stochastic quantization of the focusing Hartree Gibbs measure

\rho
constructed in Theorem
1.16
,
associated with the energy functional
E^{\sharp}(u)
in (
1.59
).
More precisely, we study
the following focusing Hartree stochastic nonlinear heat equation (SNLH) on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
:

\displaystyle\partial_{t}u+(1-\Delta)u-\sigma(V\ast:\!u^{2}\!:)u+M_{\gamma}(:\!u^{2}\!:)u=\sqrt{2}\xi,

(A.1)

where
\sigma>0
and
M_{\gamma}
is as in (
2.2
).

Theorem A.1
.

Let
\sigma>0
.
Let
V
be the Bessel potential of order
\beta\geq 2
,
where
we also assume that
\sigma>0
is sufficiently small
when
\beta=2
.
Then, the focusing Hartree SNLH (
A.1
)
on the three-dimensional torus
\mathbb{T}^{3}

is almost surely globally well-posed
with respect to the random initial data distributed
by the focusing Hartree Gibbs measure
\rho
in (
1.53
).
Furthermore, the Gibbs measure
\rho
is invariant under the resulting dynamics.

Here, we made a somewhat informal statement in the spirit of Theorem
1.3
.
A rigorous statement needs to be given in terms
of a limiting procedure as in
Theorem
2.1
, which we omit.

As in the wave case,
the main task is to prove local well-posedness of (
A.1
).
Once this is achieved, then the rest follows from
Bourgain’s invariant measure argument
whose detail we omit.
Thus, we only prove local well-posedness of (
A.1
)
in the following.

Remark A.2
.

The defocusing/focusing nature of the problem does not play an important role
in the local well-posedness argument.
By simply setting
\sigma<0
in (
A.1
) and
A=0
in (
2.2
),
our argument below proves an analogue of Theorem
A.1

in the defocusing case
for
\beta>1
.
See Proposition
A.3
below.

In the defocusing case, by adapting
the well-posedness argument

[
24
,
44
,
52
,
61
]

for the parabolic
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-model (
1.19
),
we expect that
an analogue of Theorem
A.1

can be extended to
\beta>0
.

Let
\Psi
be
the stochastic convolution, satisfying

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\Psi+(1-\Delta)\Psi=\sqrt{2}\xi\\

Before proceeding to the proof of Proposition
A.3
,
we first recall the Schauder estimate for the heat equation.
Let
P(t)=e^{-t(1-\Delta)}
denote the linear heat propagator defined
as a Fourier multiplier operator:

\displaystyle P(t)f=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}e^{-t\langle n\rangle^{2}}\widehat{f}(n)e_{n}

for
t\geq 0
.
Then, we have the following Schauder estimate
on
\mathbb{T}^{d}
.

Lemma A.4
.

Let
-\infty<s_{1}\leq s_{2}<\infty
.
Then, we have

\displaystyle\|P(t)f\|_{\mathcal{C}^{s_{2}}}\lesssim t^{\frac{s_{1}-s_{2}}{2}}\|f\|_{\mathcal{C}^{s_{1}}}

(A.7)

for any
t>0
.

The bound (
A.7
) on
\mathbb{T}^{d}

follows from the decay estimate for the heat kernel on
\mathbb{R}^{d}

(see Lemma 2.4 in
[
3
]
) and the Poisson summation formula
to pass such a decay estimate to
\mathbb{T}^{d}
.

Proof of Proposition
A.3
.

Define a map
\Phi
by

\displaystyle\Phi(v)(t)

\displaystyle=P(t)v_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}P(t-t^{\prime})\big(\mathcal{N}_{1}(v)+\mathcal{N}_{2}(v)\big)(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}.

(A.8)

Let
0<T\leq 1
.
We assume

\displaystyle\|\Xi(\Psi)\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{1}}\leq K

(A.9)

for some
K\geq 1
,
where
\Xi(\Psi)

and
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{1}
are as in (
A.5
) and (
A.6
).

From

A.4
,
(
A.4
),
(
3.5
),
and Lemma
3.2
with (

), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\Phi(v)\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{C}^{s}_{x}}&\lesssim\|v_{0}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{s}}+T^{\theta}\Big(\|v\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{C}^{s}_{x}}^{5}+K^{5}\Big).\end{split}

(A.12)

and thus a similar computation also yields a difference estimate:

\displaystyle\|\Phi(v_{1})-\Phi(v_{2})\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{C}^{s}_{x}}

(A.13)

Therefore,
local well-posedness of (
A.3
)
follows from a contraction argument with
(
A.12
) and (
A.13
).
An analogous computation
shows that the solution
v
depends continuously on
the enhanced data set
\Xi
in (
A.5
).
∎

Appendix B
On the regularities of the stochastic terms

In the following, we study the regularities of the stochastic terms,
appearing in Subsection
6.2
.
From (
6.19
) and (
6.13
),
we have

\displaystyle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)^{-1}[(V_{0}\,\ast\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\,)Y_{N}]^{\diamond}

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\Big((V_{0}\,\ast\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\,)Y_{N}-2K_{N}*Y_{N}\Big).

In view of
(
1.39
) and (
1.40
),
we see that the subtraction of

2K_{N}*Y_{N}=2\widehat{Y}_{N}(n,t)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
n_{1}\neq-n\\
|n_{1}|\leq N\end{subarray}}\widehat{V}(n+n_{1})\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-2},

removes the divergent term
in
(V_{0}\,\ast\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:)\mathbin{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces
